title: Find Passive Candidates: 9 Sourcing Strategies (September 2026)
summary: These 9 passive candidate sourcing strategies help startups build a strong talent pool faster. See Dover's top recruiting tips. (September 2026)
body_markdown:
Building a strong candidate pipeline takes more than posting a job and waiting. Most early-stage teams waste time on reactive hiring, scrambling to fill roles as they open instead of keeping a warm bench of[passive candidates](https://www.dover.com/) ready to go. The nine strategies below give founders and hiring managers a repeatable playbook for getting in front of the right people before a seat goes vacant.


**TLDR:**


-


Two follow-ups sent 3 days apart produce the highest response rate, with 25-30% of interested candidates coming from those touchpoints.


-


Personalized outreach can increase interested responses by more than 30% compared to generic messages.


-


Niche job boards like Stack Overflow and Wellfound trade volume for fit on technical roles with specialized requirements.


-


Layoff aggregator sites give you direct access to recently laid-off tech workers, a pool that has grown considerably in 2026.


-


Some tools pair a free ATS with on-demand recruiting support at $2,000 to $7,000 per hire, with no contracts required.


## 1. Create an Ideal Candidate Persona


By using candidate personas, recruiters can better understand a position’s needs and what kind of traits will make an ideal candidate. They can also use the persona to guide job advertising and attract the right types of candidates.


Before you start your search, sit down with your hiring manager and draft an ideal candidate profile; consider things like:


-


Prior work experience


-


Field of study


-


College attended


-


Industries they have experience in


-


How they communicate


-


How they manage and collaborate with people


For interviewing, having a shared understanding of the candidate persona helps guide conversations and elicit responses that accurately assess each candidate’s skills. This helps your hiring team make more informed decisions about the type of person they’re looking for, and helps more easily narrow down your shortlist of candidates.


## 2. Don’t Fumble Your Follow Up


Candidates are inundated with emails in today’s market, and many times, they likely miss your initial outreach. Looking at Dover’s internal data, we’ve seen that follow-up emails produce a sizable number of interested candidates, with 25% of interested candidates coming from the second follow-up and 30% for the third follow-up.


## 3. Post Jobs on Social Channels


Most employers use social media as a way to reach potential candidates. Post open roles on your most popular channels and create content that showcases your company culture, starting with whichever platform your ideal candidate persona already engages with most.


As expected, the top social platform for recruiting is LinkedIn, closely followed by Facebook, X (formerly Twitter), and Instagram.


Platform Best For Main Limitation


LinkedIn Broad professional reach; any role type Expensive to promote; noisy without strong following


Facebook Part-time, retail, food, or local roles Low impact without an existing company page following


Instagram Showcasing employer brand to younger candidates Requires brand awareness and visual content investment


X (Twitter) Tech and niche industries with active communities Hard to convey a full job posting in a short post


### LinkedIn


-


**Pros** : Table stakes for recruiting. Engage broadly with candidates who fit your criteria or already follow your company.


-


**Cons** : It’s expensive to promote job postings. On top of that, because of its size, it’s oversaturated with employer branding posts, and unless you have a decent following or a team dedicated to it, it’ll take a lot to stand out against the noise.


### Facebook


-


**Pros:** Strong for part-time roles in sales, retail, or food service. Demographic targeting lets you zero in on your ideal candidate.


-


**Cons:** Low impact without an existing company page following.


### Instagram


-


**Pros:** Good for showcasing employer brand to younger candidates, including those from unconventional backgrounds.


-


**Cons:** Only works if you already have brand awareness and a following.


### X (formerly Twitter)


-


**Pros** : Useful for reaching candidates in tech and niche industries if your team already has a following there.


-


**Cons:** Hard to convey a full job posting in a short post, which limits reach for early-stage companies without strong brand recognition.


One example of social recruiting in action: E. & J Gallo Winery promotes marketing roles through video content on their Instagram page, where video posts drive strong engagement and click-through. For a deeper look, see our guide on[social recruiting strategies](https://www.dover.com/blog/social-recruiting-strategies) .


## 4. Use Employee Referrals


If you hire great people, they tend to refer other great people. Research shows that referral hires[hire faster and stay longer](https://theundercoverrecruiter.com/infographic-employee-referrals-hire/) , filling roles in roughly 29 days versus 45 days through career sites, with substantially higher retention. For tips on building referral tracking into your hiring process, see our guide on[referral tracking in your ATS](https://www.dover.com/blog/referral-tracking-ats-startups) . **Your employees understand your company’s culture and are great judges on a candidate’s ability to be a reliable team member.**


Providing candidates with templates or a script they can use to reach out to their network is useful, especially since many folks feel awkward when reaching out to their own contacts. For more tips, read our blog on how to hire from your personal network without feeling awkward about it.


## 5. Find Talent With Recent Layoff Lists


With tech layoffs continuing through 2025 and into 2026, there is a larger pool of active talent open to new roles, and many of those candidates are actively looking.


Layoff aggregator sites, like layoffs.fyi or Dover’s own onesoftlanding.com allow you to access the contact information for recently laid off employees, which can be a great way to find top talent who you know will likely respond to your outreach.


## 6. Personalize Your Outreach


After you’ve narrowed down a list of target candidates, how do you get them to find your company and opportunity exciting enough to start a conversation? By writing effective recruiting emails that are tailored to their personal skills, background and interests.


At Dover, we found personalized outreach increased interested responses by more than 30%, even if the candidates responded as “not interested” to other companies.


Search a candidate’s profile for skill overlap with the role, or ask how things are going at their current company if their profile is sparse.


Examples include:


-


*I’m really interested in the project you worked on at ACME. Can you tell me more about it?*


-


*How are things going at Facebook? Really impressed with your professional growth there!*


-


*Love your experience with building an e-comm app. That will be one of your primary areas of focus in this new role!*


## 7. Build Your Employer Brand to Attract Talent


While employer branding doesn’t always produce immediate results, building your company as a place where employees are happy to work will improve the likelihood of your candidates responding. According to[Glassdoor’s 2025 employer branding research](https://www.glassdoor.com/blog/most-important-employer-branding-statistics/) , 83% of job seekers are likely to research company reviews and ratings when deciding where to apply.


When auditing your brand, you want to take a look at the following:


-


Your careers and team page


-


Your social profiles and how up to date they are


-


Employee testimonials


-


You have a clear employee value proposition


If you’re just getting started, build a careers page first. It’s the simplest way to showcase your team, culture, and benefits in one place.


## 8. Write an Enticing Job Description


Many candidates determine their fit through your job description and will usually reference it during an interview. According to an Indeed survey of over 2,000 job seekers, more than half say the quality of a job description is “very or extremely influential” on their decision to submit an application.


A good job description will include the following:


-


projects the new hire will work on or day-to-day aspects of the role


-


necessary skills and competencies


-


organization’s culture.


**Pro tip:** Keep your job descriptions concise -[Textio](https://textio.com/) recommends sticking to 5-7 bullets so candidates read the whole post. For a full breakdown of what makes a job description work, read our[job description writing guide](https://www.dover.com/blog/job-description-guide) .


## 9. Consider Using Niche Job Boards


If you’re hiring for a role with a small candidate pool, or with unique responsibilities and experience requirements, you’re better off finding niche job boards to hit your goals.[Niche boards in 2026](https://smoothhiring.com/best-job-boards-in-2026-which-platforms-actually-deliver-hires/) consistently deliver roughly 2x better candidate-to-role match rates for specialized roles compared to general platforms, so you trade raw volume for far better fit. Keep the following niche job boards in mind next time you’re hiring for tech roles: Stack Overflow,[Wellfound](https://wellfound.com/) , Tech Talent, or Geeklist.


Regardless of which strategies you use, it’s important to continuously audit your hiring process so that you optimize weak points, refine your[candidate sourcing techniques](https://www.dover.com/blog/candidate-sourcing-techniques-guide) , and save time and money in your recruiting process overall.

## Sourcing in 2026: What’s New


The sourcing world has shifted considerably over the past year. AI-powered tools are now widely used for initial candidate identification and outreach personalization, helping smaller teams reach more qualified people faster. Skills-based hiring has gained real traction among startups, with more companies dropping degree requirements in favor of proven competencies. Continued tech layoffs have also created unusually active passive candidate pools: TrueUp’s 2026 layoff tracker reports 594 tech layoffs so far in 2026, impacting over 187,000 workers. Some of the strongest talent in the market is more receptive to outreach than in prior years.


## FAQs


### What sourcing strategies work best for finding passive candidates in 2026?


Personalized outreach and employee referrals tend to produce the strongest results for passive candidates. Dover’s internal data shows personalized messages increase interested responses by more than 30%, and 25 to 30% of interested candidates come from second and third follow-ups sent 3 days apart. Layoff aggregator sites like layoffs.fyi are worth adding to the mix in 2026, given that over 187,000 tech workers have been affected by layoffs so far this year, making previously passive talent more reachable than in prior years.


### Can a free ATS handle job distribution, referral tracking, and candidate pipeline management for an early-stage startup?


Yes. Dover’s free ATS distributes jobs to 100+ boards with one click, includes native employee referral tracking with no setup required, and centralizes all candidates in a single pipeline, with no limits on jobs or users. Teams that need hands-on sourcing support can layer in a fractional recruiter through Dover’s marketplace, typically at $2,000 to $7,000 per hire with no contracts, while keeping all candidate data in the same system.


### Do I need a fractional recruiter if I’m already using an ATS?


An ATS handles the infrastructure side of hiring: distributing job postings, organizing inbound applications, tracking referrals, and keeping your pipeline visible. It won’t source candidates proactively, write personalized outreach, or run interviews. For teams with steady inbound volume and bandwidth to work the pipeline, the ATS alone can be enough. When a role is senior, specialized, or time-sensitive, a fractional recruiter fills that gap without a full-time hire or agency contract. The cleanest setup is both in the same system, so sourcing notes, candidate history, and outreach data stay in one place rather than disappearing when the search ends.


## Final Thoughts on Sourcing Strategies for 2026


No single sourcing approach works for every company, and reaching[passive candidates](https://www.dover.com/) is rarely a one-time push. The right mix depends on your hiring volume, the roles you’re filling, and how much bandwidth your team has for recruiting. What separates teams that hire well from those that don’t is consistency: building warm pipelines before seats open and treating employer brand as an ongoing investment. Dover’s free ATS and recruiter marketplace give startups a practical foundation for this without standing up a full in-house recruiting function.
